[2024], which is sample efficient when q π -realizability holds (see Theorem 2). ? Recall that if we knew G? we would simply run FQI, which estimates q π̄G? well, and then greedifies. Although we use the Õ notation to hide logarithmic factors, we explicitly write the log(1/α) factor, since it will be important to keep track of it when we set α at the end. For exposition only, we make two simplifying assumptions15 : (i) in the first claim of the lemma we have perfect estimates (i.e., ˜ = 0), and (ii) that the bound holds pointwise instead of in expectation. Together, these simplifications imply the following very useful properties: Qopt only contains the q-functions of π̄G ? ? π̄ ? π̄ under different modifications (i.e., Qopt ⊆ {q G : G ∈ G}), and q G ∈ Qopt . ? ? Based on these properties, this suggests a natural strategy for the learner. Recall that q π ≥ q π ? ? for any policy π, and that q π − q π̄G? ≤ Hα (Lemma 8). Thus, the q-function in Qopt that has the ? highest value at the start state must estimate q π (s1 ) with error at most Hα. We have also seen at the ? end of Section 4.1 that greedifying w.r.t. a good estimate of q π gives a near optimal policy. Thus, the learner should simply select the q-function in Qopt that has the highest value at the start state, and greedify w.r.t. it. Fortunately, this same idea extends to the case without the simplifying assumptions (see Appendix B). The final error is Hα + 2H˜  (see Eq. (25)), and α is set to balance the two terms. This learner is shown in Algorithm 1, and given the name L IN -q π -FQI since the construction of Qopt is related to FQI. The analysis in Appendix B formalizes the above steps.
